rewrite.question: In most chat model APIs, what is the difference between the system instructions and a user message?
options: They are interchangeable; the API concatenates them before the model sees them
System instructions set role, rules and format for the whole conversation; the user message carries one request
The user message sets the standing rules; the system instructions carry the current turn
Only system instructions are billed as input tokens
rewrite.hint: One of the two is meant to hold for every turn. Decide which, before comparing the wording.
rewrite.explanation: System instructions state what should hold for the whole exchange (role, constraints, output format); the user message is one request inside it. Swapping them buries standing rules in a turn the model weighs like any other. The shape differs by vendor - OpenAI Chat Completions takes a system or developer role message, while Anthropic's Messages API has no system role and takes a top-level system parameter - but the split is the same, and both are billed as input tokens.

rationale: The key is the only defensible answer and the objective is central to calling any model API, but the stem keys a message shape one major vendor no longer has and the hint is filler. Naming both shapes keeps the item accurate as APIs move.
evidence: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/messages - "there is no \"system\" role for input messages in the Messages API"; system is a top-level parameter
https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/api-reference/chat/create - ChatCompletionDeveloperMessageParam: "With o1 models and newer, developer messages replace the previous system messages"

rewrite.question: A chat assistant resends the whole history on every turn. What goes wrong as the conversation grows, and what is the usual fix?

rewrite.explanation: Because each request carries the whole history, both the input bill and the prompt size grow with every turn until the conversation hits the context window. rewrite.question: Every reply from your assistant must be JSON matching a fixed schema. Which approach gives the strongest guarantee?

What is constrained is shape, not meaning: the model can still pass a well-formed but wrong account id, so authorization and business-rule checks stay on your side of the call. Tool arguments are billed as tokens like any other output.

rationale: The key is right and the 'guarantees the answer is correct' distractor is already the right idea, but the explanation then drifts toward 'safely' and two options are jokes. Separating valid shape from valid meaning is the transferable lesson.
evidence: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs - strict tool use validates tool names and inputs against the schema, which constrains structure rather than semantics

rewrite.hint: The term names exactly one released artifact. Decide which one.
rewrite.explanation: Open-weight means the parameters are published, so you can run the model on your own hardware and fine-tune it. That is narrower than open source: training data and code are usually withheld, and several popular licenses add use restrictions that would not meet the OSI definition - which is why 'open-source model' is the loose usage. rewrite.hint: Ask what a leaderboard number actually holds constant between two models.
rewrite.explanation: A benchmark fixes the tasks and the scoring so two models can be compared on identical input; that comparison is the whole claim. It is not a safety certification, it says nothing about your latency or your bill, and it has no bearing on data licensing. It also only transfers to your workload insofar as your tasks resemble the benchmark's, which is why teams build a small evaluation set from their own traffic.

rationale: Pairs with rm-ai-158 and points at a decision developers actually face when picking a model, but the joke options make it unmissable. Four plausible purposes plus the pointer to your own eval set give it content.
evidence: knowledge: benchmarks standardize task and scoring for cross-model comparison; they do not certify safety, cost or licensing

rewrite.hint: Ask what happens to a public test set after it has been on the web for a year.
rewrite.explanation: Public test sets get scraped into training corpora, so a model may have seen the answers - contamination - and teams also optimize against a published metric until it stops tracking the underlying skill. That is why a leaderboard jump can fail to appear on your workload, and why a small private evaluation set built from your own tasks is worth more than a public number. Many benchmarks are open and reproducible and they cover far more than coding; the problem is what the score means, not whether you can compute it.

rationale: The most useful item in the level: it teaches skepticism about the exact numbers this topic is otherwise tempted to memorize. Only the filler hint, two weak options and a missing 'so build your own eval' keep it from passing.
evidence: knowledge: benchmark contamination through web-scraped training data and metric overfitting are documented reasons leaderboard scores fail to transfer

options: Open weights remove the need for GPUs, since the model runs on any server

rewrite.hint: Ask what you gain, and what lands on your on-call rotation.
rewrite.explanation: Running open weights yourself means the data never leaves your boundary and the model version never changes underneath you, but capacity planning, GPU cost, batching, upgrades and uptime all become yours. Hosted providers do offer fine-tuning, so customization is not the deciding factor, and self-hosting is cheaper per token only at high steady utilization - an idle GPU bills all night, while an API bills nothing.

rationale: A genuine build-versus-buy trade-off that will outlive every model named in this level, and the key states it correctly. The two new distractors replace jokes with the beliefs that actually drive the wrong decision.
evidence: knowledge: self-hosting shifts serving, scaling and upgrade work to the operator; hosted fine-tuning is available from major providers; per-token economics favor self-hosting only at high sustained utilization
